evaluations.bottleneck: Before Daniel Bernoulli's logarithmic utility, valuing uncertain outcomes had no logarithmic scoring form because expected value treated gains linearly and paradoxes like St. Petersburg had no resolution.
Before Bayes' theorem, updating beliefs from evidence was impractical because there was no rule for inverting conditional probabilities.
Before Legendre's least squares, fitting models to data was impractical because there was no simple published criterion for combining inconsistent observations.
Before Pearson's chi-squared test, judging whether observed frequencies matched a hypothesized distribution was impractical because there was no standardized statistic for distributional mismatch.

Q5.evidence: Pearson's 1900 chi-squared statistic gave a computable number comparing observed cell counts to expected counts under a model distribution.
Q5.falsification: if Shannon's 1948 derivation or early classifier losses are shown to derive from chi-squared rather than log-probability
Q5.source: Pearson, On the Criterion that a Given System of Deviations... (1900)

evaluations.bottleneck: Before Fisher's maximum likelihood estimation, fitting a model distribution to data lacked a principled objective because there was no general criterion identifying the parameters that make the observed data most probable.

Q1.evidence: Maximizing log-likelihood is mathematically identical to minimizing cross-entropy between the empirical distribution and the model, so Fisher's 1922 framework supplied the exact optimization form cross-entropy loss later used.
Q1.falsification: if maximizing log-likelihood were shown not to equal minimizing expected negative log-probability under the empirical distribution
Q1.source: Fisher, On the Mathematical Foundations of Theoretical Statistics (1922)

Q10.evidence: Maximum likelihood displaced ad hoc moment-matching and minimum chi-square as the default estimation principle in mathematical statistics.
Q10.falsification: if moment methods remained the stated default in post-1922 statistics texts
Q10.source: Fisher, On the Mathematical Foundations of Theoretical Statistics (1922)

Q11.evidence: Cross-entropy loss in classifier training is historically introduced and justified as negative log-likelihood, placing Fisher directly on the trunk line to the parent.
Q11.falsification: if early cross-entropy classifier work is shown to cite no likelihood lineage at all
Q11.source: Fisher, On the Mathematical Foundations of Theoretical Statistics (1922)

Q12.evidence: After Fisher, likelihood-based estimation never reverted; modern classifier training still minimizes negative log-likelihood as cross-entropy.
Q12.falsification: if mainstream classifier training abandoned likelihood objectives after 1948
Q12.source: Bishop, Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning (2006)

Q2.evidence: Maximum likelihood gave a single general recipe for fitting any parametric distribution, unblocking estimation across statistics and later machine-learning classifiers.
Q2.falsification: if pre-1922 practice already had an equally general parametric fitting recipe in routine use
Q2.source: Fisher, On the Mathematical Foundations of Theoretical Statistics (1922)

Q3.evidence: No ready substitute in 1922 provided likelihood's generality, efficiency theory, and log-additive form; least squares covered only the Gaussian special case.
Q3.falsification: if a contemporaneous general substitute with the same log form is shown to have been standard
Q3.source: Fisher, On the Mathematical Foundations of Theoretical Statistics (1922)

Q6.evidence: Fisher's likelihood supplied the design model — choose parameters maximizing the probability of observed data — that makes cross-entropy minimization a deliberate training procedure.
Q6.falsification: if cross-entropy training is shown to have been designed without any likelihood rationale

Q7.evidence: Likelihood became a standard modular objective that other statisticians and later ML practitioners could invoke without re-deriving estimation theory.
Q7.falsification: if likelihood had remained an idiosyncratic method used only by Fisher
Q7.source: Fisher, Statistical Methods for Research Workers (1925)

Q8.evidence: Maximum likelihood spread from statistics into genetics, econometrics, psychometrics, and eventually machine learning classification.
Q8.falsification: if likelihood's use is shown to have stayed confined to Fisher's immediate circle
Q8.source: Aldrich, R.A. Fisher and the Making of Maximum Likelihood 1912-1922 (1997)

evaluations.bottleneck: Before Napier's logarithms, computing with products and powers of probabilities was impractical because multiplication of many small numbers had no additive representation.

Q1.evidence: Logarithms converted multiplication into addition, making quantities like the log-probability of a sequence — the core of cross-entropy — computable and even conceivable as a sum at all.
Q1.falsification: if an additive representation of products in routine pre-1614 use is shown to have served the same role

Q10.evidence: Logarithmic computation displaced direct long multiplication and prosthaphaeresis as the default for large calculations within a generation.
Q10.falsification: if practitioners continued preferring direct multiplication after log tables were available

Q11.evidence: Cross-entropy is defined as an expected negative logarithm; remove the logarithm and the 1948 measure does not exist in any form.
Q11.falsification: if the 1948 cross-entropy measure is shown to be statable without logarithms
Q11.source: Shannon, A Mathematical Theory of Communication (1948)

Q12.evidence: Logarithms were never displaced as the basis of information and likelihood measures; entropy is still defined with a logarithm today.
Q12.falsification: if information theory later adopted a non-logarithmic entropy as standard
Q12.source: Cover and Thomas, Elements of Information Theory (2006)

Q2.evidence: Once log-probability exists as an additive quantity, entropy, cross-entropy, likelihood, and information measures all become definable from it.
Q2.falsification: if Shannon's entropy is shown to be definable and used without logarithms
Q2.source: Shannon, A Mathematical Theory of Communication (1948)

Q3.evidence: No pre-1614 substitute gave an additive measure of multiplicative quantities; prosthaphaeresis was a narrow trigonometric trick, not a general log function.
Q3.falsification: if a general pre-Napier log-equivalent is documented in practical use

Q4.evidence: Log tables reduced multi-digit multiplication and exponentiation from long hand computation to table lookup and addition, an order-of-magnitude saving Kepler and astronomers attested to.
Q4.falsification: if contemporary users reported no substantial time saving from log tables

Q6.evidence: The logarithm supplied the functional form — additive over independent events, monotonic in probability — that Shannon in 1948 required his information measure to satisfy.
Q6.falsification: if Shannon's axioms are shown to select a non-logarithmic measure
Q6.source: Shannon, A Mathematical Theory of Communication (1948)

Q7.evidence: Logarithms became a universal standard module in tables, slide rules, and later software, used without understanding their construction.
Q7.falsification: if logarithms had remained a specialist technique rather than standard computational infrastructure

Q8.evidence: Logarithms spread from astronomy into navigation, engineering, statistics, acoustics, and information theory, far beyond their computational home field.
Q8.falsification: if logarithm use is shown to have stayed within astronomy

evaluations.bottleneck: Before Huygens's mathematical expectation, averaging a quantity over uncertain outcomes was impossible in principled form because probability had no expectation operator.

Q11.evidence: Remove expectation and neither entropy nor cross-entropy — both defined as expected values — can be stated; Huygens sits on the direct trunk.
Q11.falsification: if the 1948 measure is shown to rest on a non-expectation averaging notion
Q11.source: Huygens, De Ratiociniis in Ludo Aleae (1657)

Q12.evidence: Expectation has remained the foundational averaging operation of probability from 1657 through modern loss functions.
Q12.falsification: if probability theory later replaced expectation as its basic average
Q12.source: Cover and Thomas, Elements of Information Theory (2006)

Q2.evidence: Expectation over a distribution is the outer operation of cross-entropy, H(p,q) = E_p[-log q]; Huygens's 1657 expected value made every later expected-loss quantity definable.
Q2.falsification: if cross-entropy is shown to be definable without averaging -log q over the true distribution
Q2.source: Huygens, De Ratiociniis in Ludo Aleae (1657)

Q3.evidence: No substitute for mathematical expectation existed in 1657; fair-price reasoning in games of chance was the only route to a probability-weighted average.
Q3.falsification: if an equivalent expectation concept is documented in routine use before 1657
Q3.source: Huygens, De Ratiociniis in Ludo Aleae (1657)

Q5.evidence: Expectation made the average value of an uncertain quantity a single computable number, the template for expected negative log-probability.
Q5.falsification: if Huygens's treatise contains no probability-weighted average of outcomes
Q5.source: Huygens, De Ratiociniis in Ludo Aleae (1657)

Q6.evidence: Cross-entropy is deliberately built as an expectation: Shannon's entropy averages -log p over the distribution, directly following the expectation model.
Q6.falsification: if Shannon's entropy is shown not to be an expected value
Q6.source: Shannon, A Mathematical Theory of Communication (1948)

Q7.evidence: Expectation became a standard operator (E[·]) used across probability and statistics without re-derivation.
Q7.falsification: if expectation remained confined to gambling problems

Q8.evidence: Expectation spread from games of chance to insurance, finance, physics, and decision theory.
Q8.falsification: if expectation is shown to have had no use outside gambling

evaluations.bottleneck: Before Bernoulli's Ars Conjectandi and law of large numbers, connecting probabilities to observed frequencies was unjustified because there was no theorem that sample averages converge to expectations.
Before De Moivre's normal approximation, computing binomial probabilities for large numbers of trials was impractical because direct summation of binomial terms was infeasible by hand.
Before Gauss's normal error law, least squares lacked a probabilistic justification because errors had no assumed distribution from which the fitting criterion followed.
Before Clausius's entropy, heat processes had no state quantity measuring irreversibility because thermodynamics lacked a named, defined entropy function.

Q8.evidence: Clausius's entropy concept traveled from steam-engine thermodynamics into chemistry, statistical mechanics, and eventually information theory, which borrowed the name and concept.
Q8.falsification: if Shannon is shown to have taken neither the name nor the concept of entropy from thermodynamics
Q8.source: Clausius, Über verschiedene für die Anwendung bequeme Formen der Hauptgleichungen der mechanischen Wärmetheorie (1865)

evaluations.bottleneck: Before Maxwell's velocity distribution, gas behavior could not be treated probabilistically at the molecular level because no distribution over molecular velocities had been derived.
Before Boltzmann's entropy formula, entropy had no probabilistic definition because macroscopic entropy was not connected to the logarithm of the number of microstates.

Q10.evidence: The probabilistic interpretation displaced purely macroscopic readings of entropy within statistical mechanics.
Q10.falsification: if statistical mechanics continued to treat entropy as non-probabilistic after 1877
Q10.source: Gibbs, Elementary Principles in Statistical Mechanics (1902)

Q11.evidence: Shannon entropy is Boltzmann's log-probability entropy generalized from microstates to messages, and cross-entropy is its two-distribution form.
Q11.falsification: if the line from Boltzmann through Gibbs to Shannon is shown to be absent from the historical record
Q11.source: Shannon, A Mathematical Theory of Communication (1948)

Q12.evidence: Entropy has remained a log-probability quantity in physics and information theory ever since Boltzmann.
Q12.falsification: if either field later abandoned the log-probability definition of entropy
Q12.source: Cover and Thomas, Elements of Information Theory (2006)

Q2.evidence: Boltzmann's S = k log W made entropy a logarithm of a count/probability, the exact conceptual move Shannon generalized to -sum p log p and hence to cross-entropy.
Q2.falsification: if Shannon's entropy is shown to owe nothing to the probabilistic entropy tradition Boltzmann founded
Q2.source: Boltzmann, Über die Beziehung zwischen dem zweiten Hauptsatze der mechanischen Wärmetheorie und der Wahrscheinlichkeitsrechnung (1877)

Q3.evidence: No substitute in 1877 expressed entropy probabilistically; Clausius's definition was macroscopic and gave no log-of-probability form for Shannon to generalize.
Q3.falsification: if another pre-1877 source already defined entropy as a logarithm of probability
Q3.source: Boltzmann, Über die Beziehung zwischen dem zweiten Hauptsatze der mechanischen Wärmetheorie und der Wahrscheinlichkeitsrechnung (1877)

Q5.evidence: S = k log W made entropy measurable from microstate counts, turning entropy into a quantity computed from probabilities.
Q5.falsification: if Boltzmann's formula provided no route from microstate counting to entropy values

Q6.evidence: Boltzmann supplied the explanatory model — entropy as log-probability of a macrostate — that made Shannon's information entropy a deliberate generalization rather than a guess.
Q6.falsification: if Shannon's design of entropy is shown to be independent of the statistical-mechanics model
Q6.source: Shannon, A Mathematical Theory of Communication (1948)

Q8.evidence: Boltzmann's probabilistic entropy reached beyond physics into chemistry, biology, and information theory.
Q8.falsification: if Boltzmann entropy is shown to have stayed inside gas theory
Q8.source: Jaynes, Information Theory and Statistical Mechanics (1957)

evaluations.bottleneck: Before Gibbs's statistical mechanics, entropy for an arbitrary probability distribution over states was undefined because entropy existed only for specific physical systems, not as -sum p log p over any distribution.

Q1.evidence: Gibbs entropy, -k sum p_i log p_i, is formally identical to Shannon entropy and, with two distributions, to cross-entropy; it made a distributional log-loss quantity exist for the first time.
Q1.falsification: if Gibbs's 1902 text contains no entropy expressed as a sum of p log p over states
Q1.source: Gibbs, Elementary Principles in Statistical Mechanics (1902)

Q11.evidence: Cross-entropy is the Gibbs/Shannon entropy functional evaluated between two distributions; removing Gibbs breaks the documented Boltzmann-Gibbs-Shannon trunk.
Q11.falsification: if Shannon is shown to have derived -sum p log p with no connection to the Gibbs tradition
Q11.source: Gibbs, Elementary Principles in Statistical Mechanics (1902)

Q12.evidence: The -sum p log p form has never been displaced since 1902; it remains the definition of entropy and the basis of cross-entropy.
Q12.falsification: if a different entropy functional later became the standard definition
Q12.source: Cover and Thomas, Elements of Information Theory (2006)

Q2.evidence: By defining entropy for any ensemble distribution, Gibbs unblocked the transfer of entropy from physics to any probabilistic system, including Shannon's message sources.
Q2.falsification: if Gibbs entropy is shown to apply only to one specific physical system
Q2.source: Gibbs, Elementary Principles in Statistical Mechanics (1902)

Q3.evidence: No pre-1902 substitute stated entropy as a functional of an arbitrary probability distribution; Boltzmann's form covered equiprobable microstates of a macrostate.
Q3.falsification: if an earlier author is shown to have published the general -sum p log p entropy
Q3.source: Gibbs, Elementary Principles in Statistical Mechanics (1902)

Q5.evidence: Gibbs entropy made the uncertainty of any specified distribution a computable number from its probabilities alone.
Q5.falsification: if Gibbs entropy cannot be computed from a distribution's probabilities
Q5.source: Gibbs, Elementary Principles in Statistical Mechanics (1902)

Q6.evidence: Gibbs supplied the ensemble design model — a system as a distribution over states with entropy -sum p log p — that Shannon's source model directly parallels.
Q6.falsification: if Shannon's source entropy is shown to share no structure with Gibbs's ensemble entropy
Q6.source: Jaynes, Information Theory and Statistical Mechanics (1957)

Q7.evidence: The Gibbs entropy formula became a standard module quoted across physics and later information theory without re-derivation.
Q7.falsification: if the -sum p log p formula had to be re-derived independently in each field
Q7.source: Tolman, The Principles of Statistical Mechanics (1938)

Q8.evidence: Gibbs's framework spread from physics into chemistry and, via Shannon and Jaynes, into information theory and machine learning.
Q8.falsification: if Gibbs's methods are shown to have had no influence outside physics
Q8.source: Jaynes, Information Theory and Statistical Mechanics (1957)

evaluations.bottleneck: Before Hartley's logarithmic measure of information, the amount of information in a message had no quantitative measure because no one had defined information as proportional to the logarithm of the number of possible sequences.

Q1.evidence: Hartley's 1928 H = n log s made information a measurable quantity for the first time, the direct problem Shannon generalized into entropy and cross-entropy.
Q1.falsification: if a quantitative logarithmic information measure is documented before 1928

Q10.evidence: Hartley's quantitative measure displaced qualitative, psychology-based notions of information in engineering practice at Bell Labs.
Q10.falsification: if Bell Labs engineering continued to treat information only qualitatively after 1928

Q11.evidence: Hartley is Shannon's cited immediate predecessor; remove it and the 1948 paper loses the measure it explicitly generalizes to entropy and cross-entropy.
Q11.falsification: if Shannon's 1948 paper does not cite or build on Hartley
Q11.source: Shannon, A Mathematical Theory of Communication (1948)

Q12.evidence: Logarithmic information measures were never abandoned after 1928; Hartley entropy remains the uniform-case standard.
Q12.falsification: if information theory later reverted to non-logarithmic measures
Q12.source: Cover and Thomas, Elements of Information Theory (2006)

Q2.evidence: Hartley's measure unblocked quantitative communication theory — channel capacity and coding — within which Shannon defined entropy and relative entropy/cross-entropy.
Q2.falsification: if Shannon's 1948 theory is shown to make no use of Hartley's framework
Q2.source: Shannon, A Mathematical Theory of Communication (1948)

Q3.evidence: Shannon explicitly built on Hartley as the predecessor measure; no rival 1928 information measure offered a substitute path.
Q3.falsification: if Shannon is shown to have relied on a different predecessor measure instead of Hartley's
Q3.source: Shannon, A Mathematical Theory of Communication (1948)

Q5.evidence: Hartley's formula assigned a definite number of units (later bits) to a message from its symbol count and alphabet size.
Q5.falsification: if Hartley's formula yields no numerical information quantity

Q6.evidence: Hartley supplied the design model — information as log of the number of possible sequences — that Shannon deliberately extended from uniform to arbitrary distributions, yielding cross-entropy's form.
Q6.falsification: if Shannon's generalization is shown not to proceed from Hartley's log-count model
Q6.source: Shannon, A Mathematical Theory of Communication (1948)

Q7.evidence: Hartley's measure became the standard special case (uniform distributions) still taught as Hartley entropy within information theory.
Q7.falsification: if Hartley's measure disappeared from information theory after 1948
Q7.source: Cover and Thomas, Elements of Information Theory (2006)

evaluations.bottleneck: Before Briggs's Arithmetica Logarithmica, logarithms were impractical for general computation because no comprehensive base-10 tables existed.

Q4.evidence: Briggs's 1624 tables of base-10 logarithms to 14 places turned log computation into fast lookup for working astronomers and navigators.
Q4.falsification: if Briggs's tables are shown to have been no faster than direct computation for users

evaluations.bottleneck: Before Oughtred's slide rule, rapid approximate multiplication was impractical because log tables required slow manual lookup for every operation.

Q4.evidence: The slide rule collapsed multiplication and division to a single sliding motion, cutting calculation time by orders of magnitude for engineers for three centuries.
Q4.falsification: if slide rule users are shown to have been no faster than table users
Q4.source: Oughtred, Circles of Proportion and the Horizontal Instrument (1632)

evaluations.bottleneck: Before the Pascaline, arithmetic was entirely manual because no mechanical device performed addition and subtraction with automatic carry.
Before Babbage's Difference Engine, producing mathematical tables was error-prone and slow because tables were computed and typeset entirely by hand.

Before Hollerith's tabulating machine, counting and cross-tabulating census-scale data was impractical because hand tallying the 1890 US census was projected to take longer than the interval to the next census.

Q4.evidence: Hollerith's machines cut the 1890 census tabulation from a projected near-decade of hand work to about a year, an order-of-magnitude cost and time collapse in data counting.
Q4.falsification: if 1890 census tabulation times are shown to be comparable to hand tallying

Q9.evidence: Punched-card tabulation collapsed the data-processing cycle from years to months, enabling repeated large-scale statistical tabulations.
Q9.falsification: if census processing cycle times did not fall after Hollerith's adoption

evaluations.bottleneck: Before Kepler's Rudolphine Tables, predicting planetary positions accurately was impractical because existing tables accumulated large errors from pre-Copernican models.
